lessons.title: Understanding Saponification Values
lessons.body: Saponification is the chemical reaction that turns oils and lye into soap. Every oil has a unique SAP valueâthe amount of lye needed to fully turn that oil into soap. If you use too little lye, your soap will be greasy and soft. Too much lye, and it will burn your skin. In Africa, we commonly use palm oil, coconut oil, shea butter, and castor oil. Each has a different SAP value. For example, coconut oil has a SAP value of 0.190 (NaOH) or 0.257 (KOH). That means for every 1 gram of coconut oil, you need 0.190 grams of NaOH to saponify it. Palm oil is around 0.141 (NaOH), shea butter 0.128 (NaOH), and castor oil 0.1286 (NaOH). You can find SAP value charts online or in soapmaking books. Always use the SAP value for the exact oil you have, because values can vary slightly by region and processing. To calculate lye for a recipe, multiply the weight of each oil by its SAP value, then add them up. For example, if you use 500g coconut oil, 300g palm oil, and 200g shea butter, the lye needed is: (500Ã0.190) + (300Ã0.141) + (200Ã0.128) = 95 + 42.3 + 25.6 = 162.9g NaOH. This is the exact amount to fully saponify. But you never use the exact amountâyou always discount lye slightly (superfat) to ensure no free lye remains. In Africa, where scales may be basic, always use a digital scale accurate to 1 gram. Never guess. If you change oils, recalculate. This is the foundation of safe soap.

lessons.title: Using a Lye Calculator
lessons.body: A lye calculator is a toolâonline or appâthat does the math for you. You enter your oils, their weights, and your desired superfat percentage, and it tells you exactly how much lye and water to use. Popular free calculators include SoapCalc.net, Bramble Berryâs calculator, and the Soapmaking Friend app. If you donât have internet, you can use a spreadsheet or even a printed chart. To use a lye calculator, first list your oils and their weights in grams. For example: 500g coconut oil, 300g palm oil, 200g shea butter. Next, choose your superfatâtypically 5% for beginners. Then select your lye type: NaOH for bar soap, KOH for liquid soap. The calculator will output the exact grams of lye and water. For the above recipe with 5% superfat, youâd get about 155g NaOH and 380g water (depending on water discount). Always double-check the calculatorâs settings: make sure itâs set to grams, not ounces, and that the superfat is correct. In Africa, where internet may be spotty, save a screenshot or write down the results. Also, many calculators let you save recipes. Use that feature. If you donât have a calculator, you can do it manually with SAP values, but a calculator reduces errors. Remember: lye calculators are not optionalâthey are safety tools. Never make soap without one. Practice with a simple recipe until you trust the process. Then you can experiment with different oils and superfat levels.

lessons.title: Formulating for Different Skin Types
lessons.body: Different skin types need different soap formulas. In Africa, we have diverse skinâfrom oily to dry, sensitive to normal. For oily skin, use more coconut oil (up to 30%) and less superfat (3-5%). Coconut oil cleanses deeply but can be drying. Add 10% castor oil for lather and 20% shea butter for conditioning. For dry skin, reduce coconut oil to 15% and increase shea butter or cocoa butter to 30%. Use a higher superfat (7-10%) to leave more oils on the skin. For sensitive skin, avoid fragrance and essential oils, or use only mild ones like lavender or chamomile. Use olive oil as your main oil (50-70%)âitâs gentle. For normal skin, a balanced recipe: 30% coconut oil, 30% palm oil, 30% olive oil, 10% shea butter, with 5% superfat. For acne-prone skin, add tea tree oil (1%) and use charcoal or clay. For mature skin, add 5% avocado oil or baobab oilârich in vitamins. Always test a small batch on your own skin before selling. In Africa, many people prefer soap that lathers well, so include coconut oil. But if you use too much, it strips natural oils. Listen to your customers. If they complain of dryness, increase superfat or shea butter. If they say soap is too soft, add more hard oils like palm or cocoa butter. Formulating is about balance. Start with a base recipe, then adjust one oil at a time. Keep notes. Your goal is soap that cleans without harming.

lessons.title: Balancing Hard and Soft Oils
lessons.body: Hard oilsâlike coconut, palm, shea, and cocoa butterâmake soap hard and long-lasting. Soft oilsâlike olive, sunflower, canola, and castorâmake soap conditioning and mild. A good bar soap needs a balance: typically 40-60% hard oils and 40-60% soft oils. If you use too many hard oils, soap will be brittle and may crack. Too many soft oils, and it will be soft and melt quickly. In Africa, palm oil is common and cheapâitâs a hard oil that gives a stable bar. Coconut oil is also hard and gives big lather, but limit to 30% to avoid dryness. Shea butter is hard but conditioning; use 10-20%. For soft oils, olive oil is excellent but can make soap soft if over 60%. Sunflower oil is cheap and makes a mild soap; use up to 20%. Castor oil (5-10%) boosts lather and is a soft oil. A classic balanced recipe: 30% coconut oil, 30% palm oil, 30% olive oil, 10% shea butter. Thatâs 60% hard, 40% soft. If you want a harder bar, increase palm to 35% and reduce olive to 25%. If you want a milder bar, increase olive to 40% and reduce coconut to 20%. Always calculate lye based on the exact oils. Also, hard oils often need more water, so adjust water discount. Test your bars: they should be hard after 24 hours and fully cured in 4-6 weeks. In hot African climates, softer soaps may melt, so lean toward more hard oils. But donât sacrifice mildness. Balance is key.

lessons.title: Superfatting and Water Discounts
lessons.body: Superfatting means using less lye than needed to saponify all your oils. This leaves some free oils in the soap, making it milder and more conditioning. A typical superfat is 5%âthat means you use 95% of the lye calculated. For dry skin, use 7-10%. For oily skin, 3-5%. To calculate superfat, multiply your lye amount by (1 - superfat%). For example, if your recipe needs 160g NaOH for 0% superfat, at 5% superfat you use 160 Ã 0.95 = 152g. Always use a lye calculator to avoid mistakes. Water discount means using less water than the standard amount. Standard water is about 38% of oil weight (or a 2:1 water to lye ratio). A water discount of 33% (1.5:1 ratio) makes a harder bar that cures faster and shrinks less. But too little water can cause soap to seize or crack. For beginners, start with a 2:1 water to lye ratio. For example, if you use 150g NaOH, use 300g water. For a water discount, use 1.5:1âso 225g water. In Africa, where humidity is high, a water discount helps soap harden faster. But if you use too little water, you may not dissolve lye fully. Always add lye to water slowly, stirring until clear. Never add water to lye. Superfat and water discount work together: higher superfat may need slightly more water to avoid a soft bar. Test small batches. Keep records. Adjust based on your climate and oils.

lessons.title: Scaling Recipes Up and Down
lessons.body: Scaling a soap recipe means changing the batch size while keeping the same proportions. This is essential when you move from a small test batch to a large production batch. The easiest way is to use a lye calculator that allows you to change the total oil weight. For example, if your recipe uses 1000g oils and you want to make 5000g, multiply every ingredient by 5. But be careful: lye and water amounts must also scale, and you must recalculate using the calculator to ensure accuracy. Never just multiply lye by 5 without checkingâbecause superfat and water discount are percentages, they scale automatically if you use the calculator. For manual scaling, multiply each oil weight by the scaling factor, then recalculate lye using SAP values or a calculator. For example, original recipe: 300g coconut, 300g palm, 400g olive, 100g shea (total 1100g). To make 5500g, multiply by 5: 1500g coconut, 1500g palm, 2000g olive, 500g shea. Then recalculate lye. Always use a digital scale that can handle large weights. For small batches, like 500g total oils, use a scale accurate to 0.1g. When scaling down, round carefullyâtoo much rounding can throw off the balance. In Africa, many soapmakers start with 1kg batches and scale up to 10kg or more. Use a large pot and stick blender. Remember: scaling up doesnât change cure time or superfat. But larger batches generate more heat, so you may need to insulate less. Always test a small batch of any new scaled recipe before selling. Keep notes on scaling factors. This skill lets you grow your business efficiently.

quiz.q: What is the SAP value of coconut oil (NaOH)?
quiz.explanation: Coconut oil has a NaOH SAP value of 0.190.

quiz.q: Why should you never use the exact lye amount calculated from SAP values?
options: A) It makes soap too hard
B) It leaves free lye that can burn skin
C) It causes too much lather
D) It makes soap too soft
quiz.explanation: Using exact lye leaves no superfat, so free lye can irritate or burn skin.

quiz.q: Which tool is essential for accurate lye calculation?
quiz.explanation: A digital scale accurate to 1 gram is needed to weigh oils and lye precisely.

quiz.q: What does a lye calculator output?
quiz.explanation: A lye calculator gives the exact grams of lye and water based on your oils and superfat.

quiz.q: If you have no internet, how can you calculate lye?
options: B) Use a printed chart or spreadsheet
quiz.explanation: A printed SAP chart or spreadsheet allows manual calculation without internet.

quiz.q: What superfat percentage is recommended for beginners?
quiz.explanation: 5% superfat is a safe starting point for mild soap.

quiz.q: Which lye type is used for bar soap?
quiz.explanation: NaOH (sodium hydroxide) is used for solid bar soap.

quiz.q: For oily skin, what superfat range is best?
quiz.explanation: Lower superfat (3-5%) helps avoid excess oils on oily skin.

quiz.q: Which oil is best for sensitive skin?
quiz.explanation: Olive oil is gentle and mild, ideal for sensitive skin.

quiz.q: What percentage of coconut oil is recommended for dry skin?
quiz.explanation: Reducing coconut oil to 15% helps prevent dryness.

quiz.q: Which additive is good for acne-prone skin?
quiz.explanation: Tea tree oil has antibacterial properties helpful for acne.

quiz.q: What is a balanced ratio of hard to soft oils?
quiz.explanation: A balance of 40-60% hard and 40-60% soft oils gives a good bar.

quiz.q: Which is a hard oil?
quiz.explanation: Palm oil is a hard oil that makes soap firm.

quiz.q: What happens if you use too many soft oils?
options: B) Soap becomes soft and melts quickly
quiz.explanation: Excess soft oils result in a soft bar that doesn't last long.

quiz.q: Which soft oil boosts lather?
quiz.explanation: Castor oil is a soft oil that increases lather.

quiz.q: In hot African climates, what should you lean toward?
quiz.explanation: More hard oils help soap stay firm in high temperatures.

quiz.q: What does superfatting mean?
options: A) Using more lye than needed
B) Using less lye than needed
quiz.explanation: Superfatting means using less lye so some oils remain free.

quiz.q: If a recipe needs 160g NaOH at 0% superfat, how much for 5% superfat?
What is a standard water to lye ratio?
quiz.explanation: A 2:1 water to lye ratio is standard for beginners.

quiz.q: What does a water discount do?
options: B) Makes soap harder and cures faster
quiz.explanation: Less water makes a harder bar that cures faster.

quiz.q: How should you add lye?
quiz.explanation: Always add lye to water slowly to avoid dangerous splashes.

quiz.q: What is the scaling factor if you go from 1000g to 5000g oils?
When scaling a recipe, what must you recalculate?
quiz.explanation: Lye and water amounts must be recalculated based on new oil weights.

quiz.q: Why is a scale accurate to 0.1g needed for small batches?
quiz.explanation: Small batches require precise lye measurement to avoid errors.

quiz.q: What happens to cure time when scaling up?
quiz.explanation: Cure time remains the same regardless of batch size.

quiz.q: What should you do before selling a scaled-up recipe?
quiz.explanation: Always test a small batch of any new scaled recipe before selling.

quiz.q: Which oil is rich in vitamins for mature skin?
quiz.explanation: Avocado oil is rich in vitamins and good for mature skin.

quiz.q: What is the SAP value of shea butter (NaOH)?
quiz.explanation: Shea butter has a NaOH SAP value of 0.128.

quiz.q: What does a 33% water discount mean?
quiz.explanation: A 33% discount gives a 1.5:1 water to lye ratio.

quiz.q: Why should you keep notes when formulating?
options: A) To remember recipes and adjust
quiz.explanation: Notes help you track what works and adjust for future batches.
